opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it changed things quite a lot. Before that, I was a pretty typical student in the Chinese system. I did fine, but my motivation came mostly from outside: the gaokao was the big target everyone was aiming at, and I was following the track because that's what you did. I didn't have a strong sense of *why* I was learning what I was learning.

Once I decided I wanted to go to the U.S. for college, the goal became mine. It wasn't something assigned to me, it was something I chose, and that made a big difference. Suddenly I cared about things I hadn't cared much about before. English, obviously, because I needed it to survive over there. But I also started thinking about what I was actually interested in, because American applications ask you to show who you are, not just your test scores.

That pushed me to explore more. I spent more time on science and on building things, reading beyond the textbook, trying to understand how things actually worked instead of just memorizing answers for an exam. It was also a bit scary, because I was stepping off the path everyone around me was on. If it didn't work out, there wasn't a clear fallback. But that pressure was motivating in a healthy way. I felt responsible for my own direction.

Looking back, that was probably the first time I learned to set a goal for myself and work backward from it. That habit stayed with me through undergrad, my PhD, and eventually into research, where nobody hands you the problem. You have to decide what's worth working on yourself.

r001.rationale: The candidate says deciding to attend college in the U.S. made the goal his own and significantly increased his motivation.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, before that decision, I was a pretty unmotivated student. I was in a decent high school in China, but I was kind of coasting. The whole system was built around the gaokao, and I remember looking at that path and thinking, I know exactly what the next ten years look like if I just keep going. And that was not exciting to me at all.

So when the idea of studying abroad came up, around my second year of high school, it kind of flipped a switch. Suddenly the game had different rules. It wasn't just one exam at the end. It was the SAT, the TOEFL, my grades over time, essays, actually having something to say about myself. And for the first time, I felt like my effort was connected to something I had chosen, rather than something that was just assigned to me.

The English part was the hardest. My English was really not good. I remember doing vocabulary flashcards on the bus, listening to podcasts I barely understood, and just grinding. But I didn't mind, because I had this very concrete picture of where it was going. I think that's the thing about motivation, at least for me. It isn't really about willpower. It's about whether you believe the work leads somewhere you actually want to be.

The other thing it changed was how I thought about what I was learning. Preparing for the gaokao, you optimize for the test. Preparing to go abroad, I started reading about what research actually looked like, what computer science was beyond the textbook, and that curiosity stuck with me all the way into grad school. So in a way, that decision didn't just get me to the US. It taught me how to be self-directed, which turned out to matter a lot more than any particular exam score.

r001.rationale: He says the idea of studying abroad “flipped a switch” and made his effort feel connected to a goal he had chosen, clearly attributing his increased motivation to pursuing study in the United States.
